Ions and their uses:
An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge. An atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion (cation). An atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion (anion). Charge = number of protons - number of electrons.

Metals usually form cations (Na+, Mg2+, Al3+) and nonmetals form anions (Cl-, O2-). Atoms do this to reach a stable outer shell, often with 8 electrons. Ions are important for nerves, bones, teeth, fertilizers and conducting electricity in solutions.
Ionic bonds:
An ionic bond is the strong attraction between a positive ion and a negative ion. It forms when a metal atom transfers electrons to a nonmetal atom.

Ionic compounds form a crystal lattice, not separate molecules. The total charge is zero, so the ions combine in a ratio that balances charge: Na+ and Cl- give NaCl, Mg2+ and Cl- give MgCl2, Al3+ and O2- give Al2O3. The name of the nonmetal ends with -ide.
Properties of ionic compounds:
Ionic compounds have strong attractions between ions in a crystal lattice. This gives them high melting and boiling points (NaCl melts at about 801 °C). They are hard but brittle, because a shifted layer brings equal charges together and the crystal splits.

Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity. When molten or dissolved in water, their ions can move, so they conduct. Many, but not all, dissolve in water.
Covalent bonds:
A covalent bond forms when two nonmetal atoms share pairs of electrons. One shared pair is a single bond, two pairs make a double bond, and three pairs make a triple bond. Examples: H2O, CO2, N2, CH4.

Most covalent substances are made of molecules with weak forces between them. They usually have low melting and boiling points and do not conduct electricity. Giant covalent substances such as diamond are very hard with very high melting points.
Conservation of mass:
The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, for example 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Balance by changing coefficients, never subscripts. Mass seems to change only when gases enter or leave an open container, so tests use a closed container.
